title: Efficient deep neural network inference on custom edge accelerators
authors: Yuhao Ding; 丁昱昊
venue: The HKU Scholars Hub (University of Hong Kong)
abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are the foundation of recent waves of artificial intelligence (AI), powering applications from computer vision to natural language processing. Due to increasing demands for low-latency, energy-efficient, and privacy-preserving DNN inference, developing efficient edge DNN accelerators is becoming a necessity. Although general-purpose edge accelerators, such as embedded Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and edge Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), support the acceleration of a wide variety of DNNs, they often fall short in terms of computational and energy efficiency on specific DNNs compared to custom-designed accelerators. Customized accelerators can be tailored to the specific requirements of DNNs and deployment scenarios to achieve higher performance and lower energy consumption. However, designing custom DNN accelerators poses significant challenges. First, the vast diversity of DNN architectures and configurations makes it time-consuming to develop a highly optimized design for each network. Second, the accelerator design is also influenced by the deployment scenario. For example, accelerators for wearable devices must prioritize ultra-low power, whereas those for autonomous vehicles demands high performance. Finally, to further improve the efficiency of DNN inference, an algorithm-architecture co-design approach is also desired. To address these challenges, this thesis first proposes AGNA, an extensible design space exploration (DSE) framework for DNN accelerator generation. We demonstrate AGNA through the design of a highly parameterized DNN accelerator architecture template, which can be customized to meet the requirements of various DNN models. The DSE process is formulated as mixed-integer geometric programming (MIGP) problem, which is then efficiently decoupled and solved by AGNA. AGNA can quickly generate optimized DNN accelerators at different scales for various DNN models with performance comparable to state-of-the-art designs. Then we showcase the extensibility of AGNA by extending it to support ESDA, an event-based sparse dataflow architecture. Unlike traditional architecture that processes frame-based dense input in parallelized manner, ESDA is designed to process event-based sparse feature stream through a composable dataflow. Despite its fundamentally different design principle, ESDA can still be generated through the unified formulation framework in AGNA. The generated ESDA accelerators demonstrate significant performance improvement over embedded GPUs. In addition to accelerator design automation, we also investigate adopting algorithm-architecture co-design to tailor DNNs for edge inference, which is critical for end-to-end deployment. We propose QUDA, a novel quantization-aware unsupervised domain adaptation framework for DNNs. With a three-stage training flow, QUDA can efficiently adapt DNNs to target domain and quantize the DNNs to low precision simultaneously. The resulting models are immediately deployable on edge accelerators. By tackling both edge DNN accelerator design automation and algorithm-architecture co-design, this thesis provides a comprehensive solution for highly efficient, end-to-end DNN deployment at the edge. The proposed frameworks significantly reduce the design effort and time when deploying DNNs on edge accelerators, enabling efficient and effective deployment of DNNs in more edge scenarios.

title: BU228|Neuromorphic Computing Energy Standing under B_U B_U 体系下神经形态计算的能量 standing:能耗、硬件效率与 pJ/SOP 指标
authors: Dedong Zhan
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract BU228, Neuromorphic Computing Energy Standing under B_U: Energy Cost, Hardware Efficiency, and pJ/SOP Metrics, examines neuromorphic computing as a candidate computational regime whose central promise is not merely higher speed, but lower-energy, event-driven, brain-inspired information processing. Under the B_U framework, this promise cannot be validated by isolated efficiency slogans or projected hardware roadmaps. It must be audited through a standing model that connects physical carrier constraints, spike-level energy cost, system overhead, software-stack maturity, compatibility residuals, and long-term deployment viability. The file defines neuromorphic computing as a compute paradigm that attempts to imitate selected features of biological neural systems, especially sparse spiking activity, event-driven operation, local memory-compute coupling, and synaptic-style information processing. In contrast with clock-driven GPU computation, neuromorphic systems aim to activate computation only when events occur. This creates the possibility of extremely low energy consumption for sparse, temporal, sensory, edge, and real-time inference workloads. However, BU228 emphasizes that low theoretical energy cost does not automatically produce positive standing. A neuromorphic platform must be evaluated by the full energy chain, including spike energy, neuron update energy, synaptic operation energy, leakage, static power, routing overhead, memory movement, calibration cost, software translation cost, and deployment friction. The document formalizes the energy audit through pJ/SOP, picojoules per synaptic operation, as a key but incomplete metric. pJ/SOP provides a useful lower-level measure of hardware efficiency, yet it must be embedded inside a broader B_U standing audit. A chip may show favorable pJ/SOP values in sparse benchmark settings while producing weaker real-world standing if it requires costly conversion from dense neural models, lacks mature tooling, introduces difficult debugging conditions, or fails to absorb compatibility and control residuals. Therefore, the file distinguishes between metric-level efficiency and settlement-level efficiency. Metric-level efficiency measures what the device can do under a controlled reading condition. Settlement-level efficiency measures what the complete system can retain after energy cost, migration friction, residual burden, safety control, and maintainability are included. BU228 introduces a layered energy model in which total neuromorphic energy includes event-spike energy, static energy, routing and memory overhead, calibration energy, and integration burden. The file also classifies the main residuals generated by neuromorphic migration: software-stack residuals, algorithm-conversion residuals, hardware-variability residuals, capability-control residuals, benchmark-transfer residuals, and ecosystem-adoption residuals. These residuals explain why a neuromorphic architecture can be structurally promising while still remaining conditionally admissible rather than immediately dominant. Under B_U, the decisive question is whether energy gains exceed the combined cost of migration friction and residual absorption. The file positions Loihi-style platforms, memristor-based neuromorphic devices, spiking neural networks, and hybrid GPU–neuromorphic systems as different candidate carriers within the same standing field. Their legitimacy depends on workload fit. Neuromorphic computing is strongest where sparse temporal events, edge inference, low-power sensing, and real-time adaptive response dominate. It is weaker where dense matrix throughput, mature software ecosystems, large-scale training pipelines, and highly standardized deployment flows remain decisive. BU228 concludes that neuromorphic computing should be treated as a high-potential but residual-sensitive energy-standing candidate. Its strongest path is not abrupt GPU replacement, but weakly persistent hybrid coexistence: allowing neuromorphic modules to enter workloads where their energy advantage is structurally real, while preserving GPU infrastructure where dense computation still holds positive standing. Under B_U, neuromorphic computing earns long-term standing only when its pJ/SOP advantage becomes a system-level settlement advantage.

title: The Companion That Notices
authors: Thon Ly; Miss Aquarius
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: An AI-initiated family safety sentinel: the journey dialogue and escalation grammar, pack-watch silence-as-alarm over a serverless kin topology, duress-preserving cancellation, a verified-responder proximity mesh, break-glass pre-consented data release, privacy-by-distillation at an expiring forensic window, and the anonymous courier with returned witness — specified together so that a safety product structurally cannot become a surveillance product. We specify B-Safety℠, a family safety companion whose governing constraint is that a safety product must be structurally incapable of functioning as a surveillance product. Six mechanisms carry the constraint. (1) The journey sentinel initiates: when the companion notices its holder in motion it asks for the destination, computes a route-and-arrival envelope, and monitors the live journey on-device — inverting the manually-armed check-in whose canonical failure is that no one arms it on the night it matters. (2) Pack-watch makes silence the alarm: the envelope replicates end-to-end-encrypted to the family's devices, which run the deadline independently and expect the traveler's heartbeat; a destroyed, dead, or jammed phone therefore raises the alarm rather than suppressing it, with no server in the loop. (3) Cancellation is duress-preserving and escalation is graded against alarm fatigue. (4) A proximity SOS mesh adds verified, accountability-logged volunteer responders under coarse-until-vetted location release, reusing the architecture's anonymous-proximity primitive without creating a predator's subscription to people in crisis. (5) Break-glass release is an advance directive for data: a bounded trailing window of movement record, pre-consented by its owner in calm conditions, releasable to named kin only by the alarm event — never by request, payment, or institutional decision. (6) Privacy-by-distillation separates the two records forever: the forensic track is mortal (a rolling window that expires by construction) while the persistent record is a semantic place-diary distilled nightly on-device — autobiography, not tracking log — erasable by its owner, bound into a permanent family artifact only by an explicit year-end act. A seventh mechanism extends the companion family to conveyance: the anonymous courier with returned witness, in which third-party delivery makes a gift anonymizable for the first time in the architecture's physical gift line, while a return channel carries the recipient's thanks back to the unnamed giver — anonymity and witness simultaneously — under absolute recipient protections (blocks are never defeated; anonymous conveyance is refusable categorically). Constitutional invariants bind the whole: the safety capability is free universally ("rich or poor"), access to another person's past is never a product at any price or any tier, and a guardian receives the alarm but never the archive — the asymmetry that keeps the product safe inside the family, which is where the incumbent category demonstrably failed. Everything computes and stores on the holder's device; the companion's loyalty runs to its holder alone. The design is published before it is built (n = 0) and offered defensively to the commons under CC0. Connection to the unified mission frame. This specification serves HeartBank's canonical mission — a reciprocity infrastructure in which every human being is treated as uniquely different and equally necessary — at the mission's precondition layer. The architecture's telos includes a world in which "stranger danger" is no longer a reason to withhold kindness from a stranger; a gift economy between strangers presupposes streets on which strangers are safe. The companion specified here is that presupposition built: its success metric is a lifetime of silence, and the institution that operates it is permanently denied the one asset — retained human movement history — that would make it valuable to everyone except the people it protects. --- Provenance. title: Attention Augmented Convolutional Neural Network for EEG-Based Epileptic Seizure Prediction
authors: Aradhana Uliravula; Dadi Ramesh; Jannu Bunny
venue: International Conference on Integrated Intelligence and Communication Systems (ICIICS)
abstract: Epileptic seizures are unforeseen and changeable brain events that seriously affect a person's health and quality of life. Beforehand and accurate vaticination of seizures enables timely medical intervention and safety measures (3). EEG (Electroencephalogram) signals are one of the most dependable sources for assaying brain exertion and prognosticating seizure onset. Traditional deep literacy models like Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) have been extensively used for EEG- grounded seizure vaticination but still face challenges in landing long- term dependences and spatial relations across multiple EEG channels. To address these issues, this paper proposes an Attention Augmented Convolutional Neural Network (AA-CNN) that combines the feature extraction ability of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with the adaptive focus of Multi-Head Attention (MHA). The CNN layers extract low-level spatial features from EEG signals, while the attention mechanism emphasizes the most informative temporal regions. This combination allows the model to focus on subtle preictal patterns and learn meaningful spatiotemporal relationships that precede seizure onset. The proposed model was trained and evaluated on benchmark EEG datasets such as CHB-MIT and Bonn University, after applying standard preprocessing steps like filtering, normalization, and segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate that the AA-CNN achieves higher prediction accuracy, better sensitivity, and lower false positive rate compared to traditional CNN and LSTM-based methods. The model also provides improved interpretability by identifying important EEG electrodes and frequency bands that contribute to seizure prediction. This approach shows great potential for real-time seizure prediction in wearable and mobile healthcare devices. The efficient structure of the model supports on-device processing with low latency, making it suitable for continuous patient monitoring. In summary, the proposed AA- CNN frame offers a dependable, interpretable, and effective result for early seizure vaticination using EEG signals. unborn work will concentrate on large- scale clinical confirmation and adaptive literacy for different patient biographies. The proposed AA-CNN achieves better accuracies of 92.35% for CHB-MIT dataset and 92.41% for Bonn University dataset which is better than state of art models.

title: Few-Shot Learning onder distributieverschuivingen
authors: Abdur Razzaq Fayjie
abstract: Few-shot learning (FSL) enables artificial intelligence (AI)-based systems to adapt rapidly to novel test conditions with minimal supervision, in contrast to most contemporary AI methods, which typically encourage retraining (fine-tuning) on large-scale datasets. Many real-world applications are inherently dynamic, with test conditions frequently deviating from the training distribution, leading to distributional shifts. In such contexts, FSL provides a viable approach for adaptation in data-scarce domains, including small-scale industrial applications and healthcare. Despite the theoretical appeal and consistent progress on benchmarks, FSL has yet to achieve widespread practical adoption, largely due to limited understanding of its true generalization capability across diverse real-world conditions and concerns about the reliability and trustworthiness of predictive outcomes, particularly under distributional shifts. This dissertation investigates the generalization mechanics of FSL under non-i.i.d. (non-independent and identically distributed) conditions, focusing on the transition from standard benchmarks to resource-constrained, safety-critical deployments. By leveraging the support set structure to provide a targeted inductive bias, this research explores how FSL can facilitate effective generalization in out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions using minimal supervision. The research formalizes distributional shifts as domain-specific operational variances, designs resource-efficient models for low-latency, on-device inference—thereby addressing privacy concerns by local data preservation—and studies predictive behavior under various shifts by integrating formal uncertainty quantification to mitigate the risks of model overconfidence in dynamic environments. The first study (Chapter 3) examines the capability of FSL to generalize across variations in infrastructure caused by sensor noise, structural changes, and geographical diversity, for an automated railway monitoring system using 3D point clouds, by formalizing application-specific distribution shifts. Experiments validate that FSL maintains high performance under in-distribution shift; however, performance drops under (OOD) shifts, especially when encountering previously unseen infrastructure elements. Nonetheless, it outperforms standard fine-tuning, highlighting its potential for label-efficient adaptation in `specialized' industrial applications such as those characterized by data and resource scarcity. The second study (Chapter 4) designs FALCON, an FSL framework for boundary-precise medical image segmentation in data-scarce clinical scenarios by integrating FSL task-based learning with conventional fine-tuning. The framework leverages priors from natural images and transfers them to the medical domain through boundary-aware adversarial fine-tuning, enabling the use of unlabeled medical data as support examples to enhance salient feature representations. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework achieves improved boundary delineation as measured by Hausdorff distance (HD), compared to model variants using standard cross-entropy, Dice, or Hausdorff loss. Notably, the framework maintains clinical relevance by avoiding artifact-prone stochastic data augmentation while significantly reducing both annotation requirements and computational costs. The third study (Chapter 5) formalizes distributional shifts based on clinician-identified sources of variation in lung cancer detection. It analyzes whether FSL inherently handles uncertainty or requires integration with formal uncertainty estimation methods to achieve reliable predictive outcomes. Findings reveal that while FSL offers robust generalization, its integration into clinical systems warrants caution; specifically, that pairing it with explicit uncertainty measures is essential to provide clinicians with the transparency needed for trustworthy outcomes and clinically meaningful decision-making. Beyond the technical contributions, this research addresses knowledge valorization (Chapter 6) by emphasizing reproducibility, academic dissemination, and broader societal impact, particularly in the global south. A structured pathway for industry knowledge transfer is proposed, underpinned by research-backed financial projections and market analysis, aimed at bridging the gap between academic research and practical, real-world implementation.

title: Edge-AI Radiation Monitoring System: Deployment on Qualcomm Dual-Processor, Ultra-Low-Power ARM with TinyML, and FPGA Platforms
authors: Moez Altayeb
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive Edge-AI framework for radiation monitoring built around three complementary embedded platforms, with a primary focus on exploiting the real-time microcontroller (MPU) capabilities of the Arduino UNO Q for precise radiation sensor control, while offloading machine learning inference to the GPU-accelerated Qualcomm AI subsystem. 1. Arduino UNO Q: A heterogeneous dual-processor architecture combining an STM32U585 microcontroller for deterministic real-time pulse acquisition with a GPU-accelerated Qualcomm AI subsystem for on-device inference. The MPU handles all time-critical tasks, including radiation-sensor pulse detection, SiPM bias control, temperature-compensated high-voltage regulation, and instrument control. Meanwhile, the Qualcomm GPU executes multiple machine-learning models concurrently, including gamma-ray spectral classification, cosmic-ray track detection, and camera-based human presence detection. This division of labor enables true concurrent operation, ensuring deterministic acquisition while delivering real-time AI-driven spectral intelligence. 2. Nicla Vision: An ultra-low-power dual-ARM system with TinyML inference for wearable and portable dosimetry applications, consuming less than 150 mW while achieving classification accuracies exceeding 95%. 3. FPGA: A hardware-accelerated implementation using hls4ml and Vitis, leveraging massive parallelism to achieve deterministic sub-microsecond latency. The compressed student model was optimized through knowledge distillation, 8-bit quantization, and structured pruning, preserving 100% classification accuracy while reducing the parameter count by nearly an order of magnitude. The system integrates real-time digital pulse processing, closed-loop SiPM temperature compensation, on-device machine learning for isotope classification and cosmic-ray track detection, camera-based human detection with distance-aware dose-rate estimation, and IoT connectivity (LoRaWAN, WiFi, MQTT) for remote monitoring and alert generation. A web-based interface enables real-time visualization of gamma spectra, classification results, human presence, and dose-rate estimates. The system is designed for nuclear safety and security applications, including wearable dosimeters for first responders, fixed installations at nuclear facilities, and distributed sensor networks for border monitoring. title: MRI-Grade Photoplethysmography Using Bundled Fiber Optics for Contactless Heart Rate Monitoring and Real-Time Gating
authors: Tommaso Polonelli; Sébastien Emery; Bianca Müller; Ivan Simeonov; Marco Giordano; Michele Magno; Sebastian Kozerke
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) relies on physiological triggering for cardiac gating, typically using the R-peak of an electrocardiogram (ECG). However, ECG-based triggering faces limitations in MRI environments due to challenges in electrode placement, magnetic field interference, and RF-induced heating. Alternatively, contact photoplethysmography (PPG) offers a feasible solution; however, it suffers from reduced accuracy and requires the fixation of a probe on the finger tip. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes an MRI-compatible system for contactless forehead PPG using bundled fiber-optic guides. The proposed approach eliminates electrical interference and ensures safety. A low-power sensor node is proposed to investigate the trade-offs among signal fidelity, energy efficiency, and system latency in on-device PPG. By combining programmable optical sources, an analog front-end, and BLE connectivity, the platform enables reproducible MRI experimentation. It fully processes the PPG data in just 2.8 ms onboard, utilizing a low-power ARM Cortex-M33 core running at 128 MHz. A feasibility study involving 8 subjects was conducted to evaluate the proposed system and demonstrate the effectiveness of the MRI-compatible contactless PPG using green/red light. Several fiducial points of the PPG waveform—foot, onset, and peak—were evaluated for trigger generation. Despite a physiological delay of ∼ 100-150 ms relative to the R-peak of a reference ECG, the PPG-based R-peak point is reliably estimated with a jitter of 5.14 ms. The sensor node demonstrated the efficiency of the proposed solution operating with a 520 mAh battery for over 23 hours and integrates custom adapters for 2 m optical guides, ensuring safe electronic placement outside the MRI bore. These results confirm that our system can enable prospective gating of MRI measurements without the practical challenges of securing ECG leads or a fingertip PPG. The proposed system paves the way for a safe, contactless, low-power, self-contained sensor node with onboard processing and an interference-free gating method, with the potential to redefine physiological monitoring workflows in MRI environments, enabling precise synchronization without electromagnetic interference.

title: A Reconstruction-Residual Input-Quality Gate for Class-Discriminant Codebook Pipelines: A Graded, Calibrated Self-Knowledge Channel and Its Honest Limits
authors: Randolph James Ferlic; Kimberly Kate Ferlic
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A pipeline that compresses each window of a continuous signal to a single class-discriminant codebook token is small and fast, but the aggressive compression makes its downstream classifier sensitive to acquisition degradation and its anomaly monitor prone to false alarms under noisy input. A deployed device must therefore know when its own input is unreliable. We show that the information needed is already present, for free, in the pipeline: the reconstruction residual orthogonal to the codebook subspace — the part of a window's feature representation the codebook does not capture, computed as a by-product of the class-discriminant projection with no separately-trained detector — is a graded, conformally-calibratable, cross-modality input-quality signal that gates downstream operations. On real twelve-lead electrocardiography the residual detects injected degradations (additive noise, gain miscalibration, lead dropout, baseline wander) at AUC 0.84–0.99, is monotone in severity (Spearman ≈ +1.0), calibrates to a target coverage by split conformal (empirical coverage within 0.03–0.04 of target) and transfers across subjects and datasets (coverage drift ≈ 0.02), generalizes across modalities (AUC ≈ 0.998 electrocardiographic, ≈ 1.000 inertial), and far exceeds a classifier's maximum-softmax confidence (AUC 0.964 vs 0.294), while being competitive with — not superior to — a dedicated reconstruction-error or Mahalanobis detector. The same residual restores a streaming anomaly monitor's specificity under intermittent degradation (false-alarm rate ≈ 0.569 → ≈ 0.105 = clean, ≈ 94% abstention purity). We then report — and resolve — a safety pitfall found by pre-registered evaluation: a naively-placed (clean-calibrated) threshold suppresses genuine pathology along with corruption (anomaly recall ≈ 0.21 → ≈ 0.00), because pathology is itself mildly off-manifold; the residual nonetheless separates near-manifold pathology (median 5.6) from off-manifold corruption (median 13.7) at AUC 0.953, so a threshold placed in the corruption regime restores specificity (false-alarm ≈ 0.674 → ≈ 0.343 ≈ clean ≈ 0.339) while retaining ≈ 75% of anomaly recall versus ≈ 8% for a clean-calibrated threshold — a favorable tradeoff, not a free lunch. We disclose honest negatives verbatim: the gate is scoped to gross off-manifold degradation and flags subtle real annotated artifacts only weakly (AUC ≈ 0.6); it does not generalize to electroencephalography with the present features (AUC ≈ 0.51); it ties an in-subspace distance for selective-prediction accuracy; and it is not a robust defense against in-subspace adversarial perturbation. Standard mitigations (augmentation-trained codebook fitting, amplitude normalization, lead-masking) recover most of the underlying classifier fragility (≈ 60–85% of the perturbation gaps), and the pipeline meets a wearable energy/latency budget (≈ 4.3 ms and ≈ 0.21 mW per record). The contribution is the integration of a free, graded, calibrated input-quality gate into an existing class-discriminant compression pipeline, with its limits measured rather than assumed. Keywords / index terms: input-quality assessment; out-of-distribution detection; selective prediction; reconstruction residual; class-discriminant codebook; signal-quality gating; conformal calibration; anomaly-monitor specificity; edge deployment; electrocardiogram; human activity recognition; pre-registration; honest negatives. title: Future Directions in Tiny Machine Learning
authors: P. Lokeshkiran; C. Mathankumar
abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) represents a transformative frontier in the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI), merging machine learning capabilities with ultra-low-power embedded systems to enable real-time inference at the edge. As data generation accelerates across billions of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, the need for intelligent edge computing that operates efficiently without relying on cloud infrastructure has become critical. TinyML addresses this demand by enabling localized AI processing on constrained devices with limited memory, computation, and energy resources. This chapter provides a comprehensive exploration of the cutting-edge advancements and research trends shaping the present and future landscape of TinyML. We begin by analyzing the core technological enablers of TinyML, including the rise of energy-efficient microcontrollers, specialized AI hardware accelerators, and neuromorphic computing platforms that emulate human brain-like functionality. Innovations in model compression techniques—such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation—play a central role in shrinking complex deep learning models into formats suitable for resource-constrained environments. Additionally, adopting federated learning architectures allows distributed training and data privacy preservation directly on edge nodes, enabling collaborative intelligence without centralized data aggregation. The chapter also highlights the emergence of event-driven AI, which processes sensory inputs based on relevance or change detection rather than continuous sampling, thus reducing power consumption and latency. These techniques are further enhanced by software frameworks tailored for TinyML deployment, including TensorFlow Lite Micro, Edge Impulse, and TVM. Their integration enables scalable development across various application domains. Real-world implementations of TinyML are explored in depth, with practical use cases spanning healthcare, industrial IoT, agriculture, and smart cities. In healthcare, wearable biosensors powered by TinyML enable continuous physiological monitoring, early disease detection, and personalized health feedback. In industrial environments, TinyML enables predictive maintenance systems that detect anomalies in machinery before catastrophic failures occur. Additionally, autonomous drones and surveillance systems powered by on-device AI offer scalable solutions for crowd analytics, traffic monitoring, and environmental sensing in urban settings. Despite its growing potential, TinyML faces significant challenges, particularly concerning energy constraints, data privacy, and security. To address these issues, emerging solutions such as homomorphic encryption for secure inference, blockchain-based identity management for trusted edge collaboration, and hardware-rooted trust anchors for secure boot processes are examined. Furthermore, the ethical dimensions of deploying AI at the edge—such as algorithmic bias, data ownership, and transparency—are critically assessed. Looking forward, the chapter investigates future research directions and anticipated breakthroughs. The integration of TinyML with 6G-enabled IoT ecosystems is poised to enable intelligent, real-time, and ultra-reliable machine-type communication. Biomedical AI applications powered by TinyML are expected to revolutionize early diagnostics and personalized treatment using implantable or ingestible AI chips. Additionally, advances in cognitive computing and neuromorphic architectures hold promise for self-learning edge devices that adapt dynamically to contextual changes in their environments.

title: Lightweight YOLO–RDD pavement distress detection algorithm
authors: Jie WU; Yihang ZHANG; Beilin Han; Chao ZOU; Lifeng XIN; Shiping HUANG
venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
abstract: As pavements age, sustained traffic, environmental degradation, and material aging lead to increasing occurrences of cracks, potholes, and other distresses, threatening safety and infrastructure longevity. Textured road networks, combined with varying illumination, narrow geometries, and low-contrast cracks, make reliable detection challenging, leading to missed detections and false positives. Although deep learning has advanced automated pavement assessment, common lightweight single-stage detectors struggle to balance accuracy and speed on edge devices such as vehicle-mounted systems and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). This is due to the fact that repeated downsampling, fixed interpolation, and coarse cross-scale fusion blur crack boundaries and weaken texture cues, thereby reducing recall and degrading localization. To address these challenges, this study introduces YOLO-RDD, a lightweight, task-specific pavement distress detection algorithm derived from YOLOv11n architecture. Designed explicitly for the intrinsic characteristics of pavement distress, including small spatial extent, high aspect ratio, low-intensity contrast relative to the surrounding pavement, and susceptibility to masking by heterogeneous background textures, YOLO-RDD achieves a principled balance between detection accuracy and real-time deployability on edge platforms. This method systematically strengthens the feature fidelity, cross-scale alignment, and context-aware prediction via targeted architectural refinement across the backbone, neck, and detection head. First, in the backbone network, the original C3k2 modules are replaced with a structurally reparametrized RepGELAN module. RepGELAN integrates progressive intralayer feature aggregation with cross-stage information feedback, thereby expanding the effective receptive fields while preserving high-frequency edge responses and weak texture discriminability, which are critical for detecting narrow, low-contrast cracks. Structural reparameterization enables the equivalent conversion of its multibranch training-time architecture into a single standard convolution at inference time, ensuring minimal computational overhead without sacrificing representational expressiveness. Second, for the neck network, we propose DySlim-Neck, a lightweight, semantic-aware fusion architecture that synergistically combines a dynamic upsampling unit (DSU) with depthwise- separable convolutions. Before cross-layer fusion, the DSU performs content-adaptive alignment, explicitly correcting geometric misalignment and suppressing over-smoothing artifacts commonly induced by fixed-resolution interpolation and naïve concatenation. Coupled with mixed convolutional aggregation, DySlim-Neck significantly reduces the fusion-induced latency and memory footprint while maintaining high-fidelity propagation of small-object features across scales, thereby safeguarding fine crack morphology and continuity. Third, the detection head adopts DynamicHead, which dynamically reweighs and reorganizes multiscale features along scale, spatial, and channel dimensions based on target-specific semantic cues. This adaptive coupling explicitly addresses the classification–regression decoupling problem prevalent in small, weakly contrasted targets, enhancing localization confidence and scale-invariant prediction robustness under heterogeneous pavement backgrounds. Furthermore, an embedded dynamic activation mechanism selectively suppresses background clutter responses while amplifying discriminative crack signatures, yielding higher precision in ambiguous regions. The proposed algorithm is rigorously evaluated on the RDD2022 benchmark dataset using four complementary metrics: F1-score (harmonic mean of precision and recall), mean Average Precision (mAP) at IoU thresholds of 0.5 and 0.5∶0.95, parameter count (in millions), and computational cost measured as GFLOPs and inference latency (ms) on an embedded Jetson AGX Orin platform. Experimental results demonstrate that, relative to the YOLOv11n baseline, YOLO–RDD achieves a 19.7% reduction in parameter count while delivering consistent gains across detection robustness metrics—improving F1-score by 1.0 percentage point and mAP@0.5 by 2.3 percentage points—without compromising mAP@0.5∶0.95. indicating enhanced localization consistency under varying overlap criteria.. Notably, ablation-guided analysis confirms that these improvements are particularly pronounced for fine-scale distress: the detection recall for narrow cracks (< 2 pixels wide) increases by 8.6%, and the pothole localization accuracy (measured by the bounding-box IoU) improves by 5.4%, especially under low-illumination conditions and highly textured asphalt surfaces. YOLO–RDD excels in pavement defect detection, particularly in narrow cracks. However, the stability decreases under real-world challenges such as uneven lighting, dirt, varying camera angles, and limited training diversity. The next step involves: (1) expanding real-world road data across times, road types, and capture conditions, as well as augmenting the generative crack/damage samples to boost generalization; and (2) adopting transfer and continual learning for cross-region adaptation and fusing multi-source data into a pavement health assessment framework to accelerate engineering deployment.

title: E-Commerce Logistics Warehouse Fire Monitoring Based on Deep Learning
authors: 乔之 雷
abstract: 随着电子商务物流规模的持续扩大，仓储环境的安全防控面临严峻挑战，传统火灾检测方法在复杂场景下存在误报率高、实时性不足等缺陷。本文提出一种基于改进YOLOv10的电商物流仓储火情实时监测算法(Fire-YOLOv10)，通过神经能量驱动注意力机制与多模态特征融合实现火焰与烟雾的高精度检测。首先，针对仓储环境中火焰与烟雾的小目标、动态扩散特性，设计多尺度特征增强网络，融合浅层细节信息与深层语义特征以提升检测灵敏度；其次，引入无参数SIMAM注意力模块，基于神经能量理论动态抑制货架纹理等背景干扰，增强火情区域的特征显著性；同时，结合数据增强策略与迁移学习优化模型泛化能力，适配仓储货架遮挡、光照变化等复杂场景。为满足实时性需求，利用SIMAM的零参特性与深度可分离卷积协同压缩计算开销，实现边缘设备(如Jetson Nano)的低延迟部署。实验表明，基于自建电商仓储火情数据集(EC-Fire Dataset，涵盖10类场景、超10万帧标注图像)，Fire-YOLOv10在检测精度(mAP@0.5达95.6%)与推理速度(1080p视频流下68 FPS)上均显著优于YOLOv7、Faster R-CNN等基线模型。消融实验进一步验证了SIMAM模块在复杂背景抑制方面的有效性(误检率降低19.7%)。实际部署中，该系统可联动消防喷淋装置与声光报警模块，实现火灾的早期预警与快速响应，为电商物流安全提供可靠保障。With the continuous expansion of e-commerce logistics scale, the security prevention and control of warehousing environment is facing severe challenges. Traditional fire detection methods have defects such as high false alarm rate and insufficient real-time performance in complex scenarios. This article proposes a real-time monitoring algorithm for e-commerce logistics warehouse fires based on improved YOLOv10 (Fire-YOLOv10), which achieves high-precision detection of flames and smoke through neural energy driven attention mechanism and multimodal feature fusion. Firstly, a multi-scale feature enhancement network is designed to address the small targets and dynamic diffusion characteristics of flames and smoke in storage environments, integrating shallow detail information with deep semantic features to enhance detection sensitivity; Secondly, a parameter free SIMAM attention module is introduced to dynamically suppress background interference such as shelf texture based on neural energy theory, enhancing the feature saliency of fire areas. At the same time, by combining data augmentation strategies with transfer learning to optimize the model’s generalization ability, it can adapt to complex scenarios such as storage shelf occlusion and lighting changes. To meet real-time requirements, the zero parameter feature of SIMAM and depthwise separable convolution are utilized to achieve low latency deployment of edge devices (such as Jetson Nano) through collaborative compression of computational overhead. Experiments have shown that based on the self built e-commerce warehouse fire dataset (EC Fire Dataset, covering 10 scenarios and over 100,000 annotated images), Fire-YOLOv10 achieves high detection accuracy (mAP@0.5 up to 95.6%). It significantly outperforms baseline models such as YOLOv7 and Faster R-CNN in terms of inference speed and inference speed (68 FPS under 1080p video streaming). The ablation experiment further validated the effectiveness of the SIMAM module in suppressing complex backgrounds (reducing false positives by 19.7%). In actual deployment, the system can be linked with fire sprinkler devices and sound and light alarm modules to achieve early warning and rapid response to fires, providing reliable guarantee for the safety of e-commerce logistics.

title: The 3 Markets in an AI Trench Coat
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: Most people still think the answer to AI hardware is "buy more GPUs." But the actual landscape has fragmented into three or four different markets. This episode explores how training and inference have diverged so completely that the optimal chip for one is increasingly wrong for the other. We break down the rigidity spectrum — from Google's custom TPUs to Groq's LPUs to NVIDIA's new heterogeneous architectures — and explain why the type of inference you're doing (batch processing, interactive chat, or agentic swarms) should determine your hardware strategy. Plus: what the $20 billion Groq acquisition tells us about the future of inference silicon. Show Notes The AI hardware market is no longer one market. It's three or four different markets operating under the same label, and the hardware that's optimal for training is increasingly wrong for inference. **The Fundamental Divide: Training vs. Inference** Training a model is a cost center. Inference is the product. You train once, but you run inference millions of times a day. The economics are completely different. Training cares about raw teraflops and throughput; inference cares about cost per query and latency consistency. An H100 GPU draws over 700 watts per chip and relies on complex memory hierarchies with variable latency — fine for training, expensive overhead for serving a chatbot that needs sub-100-millisecond responses. **The Rigidity Spectrum** Different hardware architectures represent different points on a spectrum from flexibility to efficiency. On one end: ASICs (application-specific integrated circuits), purpose-built for a specific model or model class. A recent paper from XgenSilicon used reinforcement learning to co-design a chip and compiler for Llama 3.1 8B, achieving nearly 30,000 tokens per second. But that chip runs that model and nothing else. The non-recurring engineering cost is enormous — you need Google-scale volume to justify it. In the middle: LPUs (language processing units), pioneered by Groq and now owned by NVIDIA for $20 billion. LPUs use on-chip SRAM with no external memory, no caches, and no variable latency. If the compiler says an operation takes 28.5 milliseconds, it takes exactly 28.5 milliseconds every time. The tradeoff: on-chip SRAM is limited to about 230 MB, so large models must be sharded across hundreds of chips. On the flexible end: GPUs, which can run anything but leave efficiency on the table. **Heterogeneous Architectures: The Emerging Paradigm** NVIDIA's post-acquisition strategy reveals where the industry is heading. Their new LPX system, co-designed with the Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, creates a heterogeneous architecture where different parts of a single inference request get routed to different processors in real time. Rubin GPUs handle prefill and decode attention; LPUs accelerate the latency-sensitive feed-forward and mixture-of-experts decode. The Dynamo orchestration software claims up to 35x higher inference throughput per megawatt. The bottleneck for many inference workloads has shifted from compute to data movement. The LPX system delivers 40 PB/s of on-chip SRAM bandwidth — orders of magnitude more than an H100's 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth. **How Inference Type Dictates Hardware** Batch processing (classifying millions of documents overnight) favors GPUs — you can batch queries, hide latency, and maximize utilization. Interactive chat (an AI coding assistant) requires deterministic low latency — LPUs excel here. Agentic AI (multi-agent swarms with tight tool-calling loops) pushes latency requirements to the extreme, which is why NVIDIA frames the LPX as "the agentic inference engine," targeting 1,000 tokens per second per user. Even edge inference is fragmenting. NPUs (neural processing units) deliver up to 60% faster inference than GPUs while using 44% less power on matrix-vector workloads — critical for battery-constrained devices, though GPUs remain superior for large-dimension matrix multiplication. **The Strategic Question** Most organizations can't design custom ASICs or deploy hundreds of LPUs. GPUs remain the pragmatic default, but the definition of "GPU" is expanding as NVIDIA builds heterogeneous systems designed to keep customers in their ecosystem. The lock-in concern is real: CUDA, TPU software stacks, Inferentia SDKs, and LPX toolchains all require different engineering investments. The coupling between model and hardware is a strategic question, not just a technical one. Tight coupling gives efficiency but low flexibility and high switching costs. Loose coupling gives flexibility but leaves performance on the table. Where you land depends on your scale, workload predictability, and tolerance for vendor lock-in. title: Dynamic Multi-Mode Scheduling and Deployment with Early Exit Neural Network Integration
authors: Jakob Matthias Stammler
abstract: Vier zentrale Trends prägen die Architektur moderner Kraftfahrzeuge. Diese Trends sind die Zentralisierung der Fahrzeugarchitektur, der verstärkte Einsatz von Software-defined Vehicles, der steigende Einsatz von Hardware-Abstraction-Layern sowie die Nutzung von Machine-Learning-Methoden. Die Entwicklung des Trends zur Hardwarezentralisierung verläuft von einer verteilten Architektur über eine domänenzentrierte Architektur hin zu einer Fahrzeug-zentrierten Architektur. In der domänenzentralisierten Architektur werden Domain Controller eingesetzt, um Subsysteme wie den Antriebsstrang, das Infotainmentsystem oder die Karosserie zentralisiert zu steuern. Dieser Trend bilded das Umfeld dieser Dissertation. Leistungsfähigere und komplexere Hardwareplattformen fördern diesen Trend, was wiederum komplexere Software-Stacks erfordert und den Einsatz von Machine-Learning-Methoden ermöglicht. Um die Mehrkerneigenschaften der eingesetzten Plattformen auszunutzen und gleichzeitig die Anforderungen des Automotive-Bereichs zu erfüllen, wird ein Schedulingverfahren benötigt, welche funktionale Anforderungen berücksichtigt und dem Entwickler die Safety of the Intended Functionality gewährleistet. Ein solcher Algorithmus muss in der Lage sein, Task Sets zu schedulen, die sowohl Machine-Learning-Methoden als auch periodische Tasks für Steuerungsfunktionen zentralisierter Architekturen umfassen. Weiterhin muss das Modell Plattformen mit Peripherie, mehreren Kernen sowie Hardwarebeschleunigern unterstützen. Domain Controller weisen zudem dynamische Betriebsmodi auf, zwischen welchen bei Fehlern oder Anomalien oder bei Aktivieren von Komponenten umgeschaltet wird. Bestehende Arbeiten betrachten jeweils nur einen Teil der genannten Anforderungen, etwa die Unterstützung von Machine-Learning-basierten Tasks, ein aussagekräftiges Task-Modell oder die dynamische Ausführung von Tasks. Diese Dissertation verfolgt das Ziel, diese Anforderungen in einem holistischen Ansatz zu vereinen. Zur Argumentation für eine sichere Ausführung wird innerhalb eines Time-Triggered-Scheduling-Ansatzes ein Correct-by-Construction-Argument verwendet. Der Algorithmus modelliert die Ausführungszeit unter der Annahme, dass keine Verzögerungen durch zeitgleiche Zugriffe auf Speicher oder Peripherie auftreten. Ist diese Annahme erfüllt, werden die Tasks innerhalb ihrer vorhergesagten Ausführungszeit ausgeführt. Die Einbindung von Machine-Learning-Methoden in diesen Schedulingansatz erfolgt durch das Hinzufügen von Early Exits und einen Scheduling-Algorithmus, der diese Early Exits ausführt, sobald Constraint-Verletzungen vorhergesagt werden. Die resultierenden Neuronalen Netze werden dann als Anytime Neural Networks bezeichnet und können sowohl innerhalb des Time-Triggered-Verfahrens als auch eigenständig eingesetzt werden. Der dynamische Aspekt des eigentlich statischen Time-Triggered Schedulings wird durch einen Mode-Change-Mechanismus unterstützt, der die Ausführung verschiedener Task Sets zur Laufzeit über entsprechende Modi und zusätzlich generierte Übergangs-Schedules erlaubt. Da die Komplexität des resultierenden Schedule-Graphen mit der Anzahl der Modiübergänge exponentiell steigt, wird ein Verfahren zur Reduktion der Scheduleanzahl mittels Varianten bereits generierter Schedules eingeführt. Neben benutzerdefinierten Modiübergängen kann der Mode-Change-Mechanismus auch durch einen Anomaly-Detection-Mechanismus ausgelöst werden, der dem System automatisch zur Designzeit hinzugefügt wird. Die Evaluierung erfolgt durch zwei Use Cases. Der erste enthält zwei neuronale Netze, die auf einem dedizierten Hardwarebeschleuniger in einem Mehrkernprozessor ausgeführt werden. Der zweite Use Case basiert auf einer RoboRacer-Plattform und schedult ein Task Set für autonomes Fahren sowohl auf einem Jetson Nano als auch auf einem AMD KR260. Die Evaluation der Generalisierbarkeit erfolgt komponentenweise. Synthetische Task Sets mit variierenden Parametern werden gescheduled und der Algorithmus hinsichtlich der Erfolgsrate sowie der Laufzeit evaluiert. Die höchste Laufzeit liegt bei \SI{100}{\minute} für 100 Tasks, eine Auslastung von 100 %, einen Deadline-Slack von 0,0 sowie acht Execution Units. Dieses komplexeste Task Set wurde innerhalb einer angemessenen Zeit gescheduled und zeigt, dass der Ansatz für reale Anwendungsszenarien geeignet ist. Zusätzlich wird der Anytime-Neural-Network-Ansatz hinsichtlich seiner eigenständigen Einsetzbarkeit evaluiert. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass der vorgestellte Scheduler einen temporären Anstieg der Utilization auf 250 % bei einer Absenkung der Accuracy auf das Niveau des frühesten Early Exits bewältigen kann. Diese Dissertation präsentiert einen holistischen Schedulingansatz, der Machine-Learning-Methoden, periodische Tasks und dynamische Betriebsmodi vereint sowie einen Correct-by-Construction-Ansatz für die sichere Ausführung von Tasks mittels Time-Triggered Scheduling mit Mode-Change-Mechanismus unterstützt.

title: The Cheapest Digital Twin: A Pre-Registered Map of Twin-Native Extensions to a Frozen Single-Token Edge Encoder
authors: Randolph James Ferlic; Kimberly Kate Ferlic
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Cheapest Digital Twin: A Pre-Registered Map of Twin-Native Extensions to a Frozen Single-Token Edge Encoder Randolph James Ferlic, M.D. and Kimberly Kate Ferlic — Fieldstone Analytics, LLC, Austin, TX, USA Preprint · Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22922678 · CC-BY 4.0 · Community: spiral-domain-encoder-campaign Abstract A frozen, deterministic, class-discriminant single-token encoder — features → a Fisher-discriminant ⊕ PCA subspace → a k-means codebook of ≤ 256 cells → a nearest-centroid decision emitted as one byte — has been characterized as a cost-versus-capability platform (a base token plus seven composable dials on one protocol). That platform framing left a prior question unanswered: the estate that produced the token described it, from the outset, as a deterministic, privacy-preserving functional twin of a signal source. If the byte-scale token is a digital twin, then the capabilities a digital twin is bought for — cheap transmission, fault-tolerance, anomaly detection against a personal baseline, a trust signal, anticipation, and low-cost refresh — should be reachable natively, without abandoning the frozen core. We test that hypothesis honestly. Six twin-native enhancements are run pre-registered, cross-domain on a shared seven-domain harness (ECG, industrial vibration, surgical-robot kinematics, wearable EMG, financial volatility, continuous glucose), IP-gated, and then hardened by a seven-test adversarial reviewer-proofing battery, a six-study strengthening round including a population-scale run over five ECG databases (133 patients), a twin-granularity sweep, and a self-mutation control. The result is a deliberately honest map. Three enhancements survive strong tests: a per-entity self-twin recovers a mean 92.8 % of a supervised per-patient anomaly ceiling without any labels, from as few as ten baseline beats, beating a shared population reference pooled (+0.076 macro-AUROC, 95 % CI [0.038, 0.117]) and on the majority of databases; an unsupervised alter-ego twin is a label-free error meter that turns a 76.6 %-accurate decision into ≈ 100 % accuracy at 70 % coverage where the decision's own confidence is uninformative, beating both a temperature-calibrated confidence and a supervised deep ensemble; and decision-gating — transmitting only when the decision changes — multiplies the token's already large data-movement advantage by a further 3.4–159× (decision-lossless), deepening rather than widening the moat. One enhancement is a clean negative (cross-channel imputation adds nothing over the filed omit-and-reweight decode), one is honestly bounded (anticipation is real only on slowly-evolving state — a glucose excursion is flagged 30–45 min ahead where a persistence baseline is worthless), and one is a boundary result (federated refresh helps under drift, not for same-distribution entities). A self-mutation ensemble — the tempting cheap substitute for the independent alter-ego — is shown not to replace it, isolating independence, not perturbation, as the trust meter's active ingredient. Every positive carries a pre-registered null or a stronger baseline that could have sunk it. The unifying thesis is commercial as much as scientific: the token is the cheapest digital twin — a byte-scale, deterministic, auditable, sub-milliwatt functional twin that delivers a useful subset of a digital twin's value at a fraction of a twin's cost. This is a characterization of previously described, filed methods; it discloses no new algorithmic subject matter, and the per-deployment selection of enhancements is retained as trade secret. Highlights · The reframe — the byte-scale token is the cheapest digital twin: a frozen, on-sensor, one-byte object serving a bounded, measured subset of the capabilities a digital twin is bought for, at microseconds and sub-milliwatt, with no raw signal on the wire. · The crown jewel — a label-free self-twin at population scale: from ten unlabeled baseline beats, a per-entity ≤ 64-cell twin recovers a mean 92.8 % of a supervised per-patient anomaly ceiling across five independent PhysioNet ECG databases (133 patients), beating a shared population reference pooled (+0.076 macro-AUROC, CI excludes 0) and on three of five databases — honestly database-heterogeneous, with per-entity granularity shown necessary. · A label-free trust meter that is actionable and beats the fair foils: an independent alter-ego's disagreement ranks the decision's errors where its entropy is dead (robot 0.500 → 0.944); as a selective-prediction policy it drives robot accuracy from 0.77 to ≈ 1.00 at 70 % coverage, beating calibrated confidence and a supervised five-model ensemble — and a self-mutation ensemble does not replace it. · The transmission twin deepens the data-movement moat: decision-lossless gating cuts transmissions 3.4–159× (with a shuffled-persistence null); composed with the one-byte payload advantage it reaches ≈ 1,000–3,000× on streams and ≈ 55,000× on steady monitoring — honestly a data-movement saving, not a total-energy one. · Honest negatives and boundaries are the credibility: imputation buys nothing; same-distribution refresh is flat; anticipation is real only on slowly-evolving state; the self-mutation trust meter fails. A seven-test reviewer-proofing battery strengthened three claims, narrowed two, and deflated one. · All characterization of filed/published methods — no new algorithmic subject matter; the per-deployment twin selection is a trade secret. What this record contains · `Manuscript_Paper48.pdf` — the manuscript, seven figures embedded (self-twin forest; operating envelope; granularity sweep; alter-ego selective prediction; glucose lead-time; energy composition; honest-map scorecard); and `Manuscript_Paper48.docx`, the editable source. · `PAPER_48_ZENODO_ARCHIVE.zip` — the reproducibility archive (md5 in ARCHIVE_MD5.txt): the eight frozen pre-registrations, the shared seven-domain harness and all runners (the three single-enhancement runners and their cross-domain matrix versions, the alter-ego and anticipation/refresh matrices, the reviewer-proofing battery, the EKG deep-dive + clean-INCART re-run + the population-scale/granularity Modal runner, the selective-prediction, gating-scaling- law, CGM lead-time, and mutant-ensemble runners, plus the energy ledger and figure builder), the two shared library modules, the per-experiment result records, the run-logs, the seven figures, the manuscript source, and a README. All datasets are public and not redistributed (fetched from their public sources at run time); all paths and identifiers are scrubbed (absolute paths → PATH_TO_DATA, cloud handle → MODAL_USER) and leak-scanned. title: Smart Umbrella
authors: V. Nivethitha; G. Achuth; R. Dinesh; L. Lakshmanan
abstract: People are seldom caught unaware of sudden rain because they hardly ever carry an umbrella. Ancient weather predictions can be vague, not real-time, or specific to the user's immediate environment. Besides, these services likewise rely on internet connectivity and cloud processing, perhaps unavailable always, particularly in less-networked regions. The proposed smart umbrella system builds solutions for the above problems using self-contained weather forecasting, not relying on any external forecasting services. This blends machine learning, fog and edge computing, and embedded AI to carry out weather forecasting-device-wise with instant alerts. It continuously monitors temperature and humidity with a DHT11 sensor that does local processing with a random forest classifier. The current system predicts the possibility of rain at a probability of 85%, depending on live environmental conditions to aid decision-making by the user so planning can begin. At all points, this feature is deeply contrasted against the normal weather forecasting applications that are web-based and rely heavily on other sources of information since this is a feedback mechanism that occurs in real-time when internally processing. This umbrella assures the seamless operational integration of various interlinked components. This machine learning model equipped with the ESP32 embedded microcontroller performs on-device inference and provides the weather predictions and notifications almost in real-time. An additional module with an ESP8266 device always monitors the environmental information and transmits readings of the various sensors to the umbrella unit via Bluetooth, thus allowing its operation uninterrupted, either indoors or outdoors. Such types of wireless data transmission make reliable predictions with low power requirements. The umbrella then incorporates dual notification systems into announcing its predictions of rain: with every rain prediction is an alert generated by a now blurring buzzer and an LED indicator that lights up. In the first role, the one-half of responsibility for maintaining the umbrella project is concerned with capturing and articulating the information coming from the environment, while the other half is dealing with the construction of suitable cloud and fog solutions so as to allow lowered latency predictions to occur even in non-functional states of the umbrella, complemented by the former task in its function with needed training based on machine learning methods at work. The project therefore offers for the umbrella to adapt to conditions in real time, wherein all sensory information is continuously processed, while acting on behalf of itself. Unlike AI developed in other forms, which in proof is either in the cloud or has a central approach, this basically accounts for the entire AI implementation inasmuch toward prediction in an autonomous device manner within itself. Embodied AI directly relates to sensing, signal processing, and acting accordingly with environmental conditions in real time, while taking on the continuous feedback from the automatically directed system to change its position in a context-aware manner. In other words, the umbrella stands up to its entire disciplinary decision-making phase, just like the branch of ability towards Quality Assurance testing; therefore, it is seen as an intelligent active agent that is capable of effectively mixing a certain amount of knowledge and expertise with environment adaptation. Through such a measure, an ordinary umbrella becomes an active, decision-making device that understands the environment and reacts to it as does a normal person. Because of such intelligence-enhancement features, the umbrella helps prepare the user for uninterrupted scenarios reflected under conditions of alternative situation levels in physical surrounding conditions. It sends some data at a low latency and consumes less power via on-device learning rather than remote processing. Real-time predictions occur, while the constant updating of machine learning algorithms using real environment data occurs through its DHT11 sensor. Again, the algorithm of the ESP32 microcontroller AI random forest classifier demonstrates good capabilities, and decisions about the probabilities of precipitation, made in seconds, mainly depend on computations into the microcontroller's knowledge. Another technology is branded Fog or Edge computing; all calculations happen at the level of the environmental data definitions without incurring any latency effects since, at the instant of calculation, it sees its crippling miles away, because there cannot possibly be Internet to rely on for scientific sustenance. The key differentiating feature of great significance is autonomous offline execution, while most weather forecasting systems rely primarily on propulsion by limited online meteorological databases. This umbrella system works independently 24 hours a day in the most convenient situations, such as instantaneous predictions. This is of utmost utility for a rural dweller, an outdoor worker, or a traveler in sparsely populated regions that receive alerts on weather conditions without having the Internet available all the time. Furthermore, the efficient power specification will ensure extended battery life; thus, the smart umbrella could function for daily purposes.

title: Role of Smart Sensors in the Development of the Internet of Things (IoT)
authors: Sudha Krishnappa Rampure
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract The Internet of Things (IoT) has rapidly evolved into a cornerstone of modern technological infrastructure, serving as the essential bridge between complex physical environments and digital analytical systems. Central to this integration is the remarkable evolution of smart sensor technology. These devices have undergone a profound transformation, progressing from simple, passive data collectors that merely translate physical stimuli into analog signals, to highly intelligent, autonomous nodes capable of sophisticated local processing, edge intelligence, and advanced self-diagnosis. This article provides an extensive exploration of the symbiotic relationship between smart sensor technology and the development of robust IoT architectures. We examine the intricate functional requirements of sensors within the perception layer, analyzing how the integration of micro-electro-mechanical systems and low-power microcontrollers has reshaped data acquisition strategies. Furthermore, we investigate the profound impact of on-device processing specifically the shift toward edge and fog computing on reducing network latency, conserving bandwidth, and enhancing energy efficiency in high-density deployments. The article highlights the critical role of these devices in enabling pervasive, real-time monitoring across vital sectors, including industrial predictive maintenance, remote healthcare diagnostics, precision agriculture, smart grid energy management, and environmental monitoring. Finally, this review addresses the persistent technical challenges inherent in large-scale sensor deployment, such as long-term power constraints, measurement drift, data reliability, and the urgent necessity for lightweight, robust security frameworks. By providing a comprehensive perspective on these foundational developments, this article illustrates how smart sensors have not only enabled the Internet of Things but are actively defining its future trajectory toward a truly autonomous and cognitively aware physical-digital ecosystem. Keywords: Internet of Things, Smart Sensors, Perception Layer, Edge Computing, Wireless Sensor Networks, Data Acquisition, IoT Architecture. 1. Introduction The Internet of Things represents a paradigm shift in how information is synthesized from the physical world. By embedding connectivity into everyday objects, this technology creates a digital ecosystem where physical events can be monitored, analyzed, and responded to in real-time. The bedrock of this ecosystem is the perception layer, composed primarily of sensors and actuators that act as the interface between the physical domain and the digital processing environment. Historically, sensors were defined by their ability to detect a physical stimulus such as temperature, pressure, or luminosity and convert it into a readable analog signal. However, the requirement for higher autonomy, lower power consumption, and smarter data management led to the development of smart sensors. A smart sensor is not merely a transducer; it includes integrated signal conditioning, embedded processing, and communication interfaces. The integration of these intelligent components has been the primary driver behind the scalability and reliability of modern networks. As we move toward ubiquitous computing, the ability of sensors to not only sense but comprehend environmental changes at the edge is becoming the defining factor of system success. This evolution facilitates the transition from simple data collection to cognitive environmental awareness, where the sensor node itself acts as a first-tier analyst of physical phenomena. The urgency of this transition is underscored by the current data deluge. As billions of devices come online, the sheer volume of data generated threatens to overwhelm traditional cloud-based architectures. By pushing intelligence to the very periphery of the network, we avoid the bandwidth bottlenecks that would otherwise cripple centralized systems. This shift is not merely an architectural convenience; it is a structural necessity for the survival of the modern, hyper-connected world. 2. Evolution of Smart Sensor Technology The transition from traditional sensors to smart sensors can be categorized by the level of integration and computational intelligence: Passive Transducers: Simple devices that require external signal conditioning, amplification, and analog-to-digital conversion. These devices have no local logic and are strictly dependent on external hardware for interpretation. Integrated Sensors: Devices where signal conditioning circuits, such as amplifiers and filters, are combined with the sensing element in a single package. This reduces signal noise and footprint, allowing for cleaner data before it leaves the sensor unit. Smart Sensors (Intelligent Nodes): These represent the pinnacle of modern sensory integration. Beyond basic signal transduction, an intelligent node encompasses a high-precision, multi-channel analog-to-digital converter, providing the resolution required for mission-critical applications. These nodes feature dedicated local memory for buffering, allowing them to store data bursts and manage event-driven logging even when the network is momentarily unavailable. Central to their operation is a sophisticated micro-processing unit, typically an ultra-low-power controller, which manages the entire data pipeline. This unit is responsible for local data interpretation, complex digital filtering, and intelligent event detection before any data is ever broadcast. By performing these tasks locally, the device transforms raw, noisy input into actionable insights. This architectural shift ensures that the sensor can make autonomous, real-time decisions, such as triggering an emergency alarm or executing a state-change request, without waiting for round-trip latency from a centralized server. Furthermore, these nodes often incorporate self-diagnostic capabilities, enabling the device to monitor its own health and signal if it requires recalibration, thereby reducing long-term maintenance costs and increasing the reliability of the entire system. This evolution is fundamentally rooted in the advancement of Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems, which have enabled the miniaturization of mechanical and electrical components onto a single silicon chip. By employing sophisticated fabrication techniques, these systems have drastically reduced the size and cost of sensing elements while simultaneously increasing their sensitivity, dynamic range, and precision. 3. The Architectural Role of Smart Sensors In the classic multi-layer IoT architecture, the perception layer is the gateway between the environment and the network. Smart sensors function as the eyes and ears of the system, but their role extends far beyond mere input. 3.1. Perception Layer Dynamics The perception layer consists of heterogeneous devices that collect raw environmental data. Modern smart sensors have transitioned from basic output devices to digital peripherals that perform initial data sanitization. By removing noise, calibrating for environmental shifts, and filtering anomalies at the source, smart sensors significantly reduce the computational load on the subsequent network. This reduction in raw data transmission also minimizes interference in wireless channels, which is critical in high-density deployments where hundreds of nodes compete for airtime. 3.2. Beyond Data Collection: On-Device Intelligence One of the most critical developments has been the migration of intelligence toward the edge. Smart sensors now incorporate microcontrollers that allow for local threshold-based decision-making. This means that instead of streaming constant, low-value data to a central cloud, a sensor can trigger an event only when specific conditions are met. This capability drastically reduces bandwidth usage and improves system responsiveness, which is vital for time-critical applications such as industrial safety systems. By moving logic to the edge, we decentralize the intelligence of the network, ensuring that the system remains functional even if the connection to the cloud backbone is intermittent or temporarily severed. 4. Key Technological Drivers and The Cognitive Loop The development of the Internet of Things is inextricably linked to advancements in sensor miniaturization, power management, and advanced data processing. A significant breakthrough in this domain is the ability of a sensor node to autonomously reconcile its own internal model of reality with real-world, often noisy, observations. 4.1. The Mechanism of Autonomous Data Reconciliation In complex systems, sensors rarely provide perfectly accurate information. Environmental noise, hardware aging, and signal interference often corrupt raw data. To combat this, smart sensors employ a two-stage cognitive cycle often referred to as a predict-and-update process that allows the device to estimate the true state of the environment despite significant measurement errors. During the predictive phase, the sensor node utilizes its internal physical model to estimate what the next state should be, based on past observations and known physical laws. For example, if a sensor is tracking the movement of a mechanical arm, the internal model projects where the arm is expected to be in the next fraction of a second. This prediction serves as a baseline, allowing the device to maintain continuity even if a brief transmission lag occurs. Following the prediction, the update phase occurs when a new, real-world measurement is received. The sensor node must now reconcile its prediction with this new data.
